author: independent-education-critic (Claude subagent, pep-standard-fast-final-checkpoint-gift canonical review, loop-1 recheck)

findings.claim: The new q27's stem gives away the 403 decision and turns the item into a two-option choice. The stem says 'the API answers 403, and she signs in again with the same account', which tells the learner she ended up on sign-in. That alone rules out distractor A (she sees the not-allowed message on /admin/refunds) and distractor D (she stays on a blank page), since neither story has her signing in. The only live choice left is B against C, which turns on whether replace: true keeps navigation state (handling-401-and-403 o2). The objective the item was added for, o3 (a 403 must keep the user and show not-allowed, not sign out), is never tested as a decision; it appears only in the feedback. The stem's phrase 'Its sign-in page, as taught, ends ...' also marks that line as correct, pointing learners at handleStatus as the faulty part. Everything else about q27 is sound. The page teaches the exact handleStatus/go pattern and the 403 contract. It is not a near-duplicate: formative 'o3 403 no sign-out' and 'o2 remember the page' are one-line recall items, and q27 is a code trace. Lengths give no cue: the key is the shortest option at 78 characters against 93, 93 and 99 (0.84 of the next), and the key is shortest in only 5 of 30 items, below chance. Reading load is light. No other item's code or feedback reveals it: q08 concerns server-side 401/403, not client handling.
findings.recommendation: Take the sign-in event out of the stem and put the full sequence into each option, so both decisions stay live. Stem: 'The API answers 403. What does Mia experience?' A: 'She sees the not-allowed message on /admin/refunds and keeps her session.' B: 'She is sent to sign-in; after signing in again she lands on the home page.' C (key): 'She is sent to sign-in; after signing in again she returns to /admin/refunds, gets 403 and is sent back: a loop.' D: blank-page option as now. Then A tests o3 directly and B tests o2. Drop 'as taught' from the stem. Keep key position C, and re-run the plain-JS model.

findings.claim: The new allocation rule says items were weighted 'toward the applied skills the Final's coding work depends on (Spring and the browser client)'. The next line then says Spring is about one item under a pure day-proportional split. That is accurate: 8/30 = 27%, against 13/39 Standard days (33%) and 8/23 Fast days (35%). But being under-sampled contradicts 'weighted toward Spring', so the rule does not explain the split it describes. The new 8/5/7/7/3 split is otherwise defensible. React 7 (23%) matches its share of days, 8/39 (21%) and 5/23 (22%). Containers 3 (10%) matches 4/39 (10%) and 3/23 (13%). The 19/20 module claim holds: every React and Containers module now has an item (auth-and-review q27; containers-and-compose q28-q29; microservices-and-ci-cd q30), and integration-and-observability is the only gap, correctly excluded by scope.
findings.recommendation: Make the sentence match the numbers. For example: 'proportional to full-taught days on both tracks, adjusted so every in-scope module has an item; Spring ends about one under because its integration-and-observability module is excluded and several of its topics are Fast-skim, and Python about one over.'
